textbookText: Figure 2.5.2 The plant body of Dryopteris (Fern)

The roots are adventitious that bear root hair and root cap. They arise from the basal portion of stem. The main function of root is anchorage and absorption of minerals from the soil. The stem is perennial, short, underground and modified into rhizome. It is covered with brown coloured scales called ramenta. The leaves are petiolate and pinnately compound that arise from the upper surface of rhizome. The leaf is known as frond. Each leaf is composed of numerous leaflets or pinnae. The pinnae are again divided into small pinnules. The leaf has long petiole which ends in a long rachis that bears pinnae. Mature leaves are of two types; the fertile leaf bearing sori called sporophyll and sterile leaf without sori called tropophyll. The young leaf is rolled up with the tip in the centre known as circinate leaf.
Reproduction Reproduction in fern takes place by vegetative, asexual and sexual method.
1. Vegetative method: It takes place by fragmentation. The older part of the stem dies and decays upto dichotomy and branches get separated. Then, each branch develops into new plant.

2. Asexual method: It is the process of reproduction by the formation of spores. The plant body of Dryopteris is sporophyte. The spores are produced in sporangia which are found in sorus (pl. sori). The sori are found on ventral surface of sporophyll. Each sorus is covered by kidney shaped protective covering called indusium that contains numerous sporangia. Each sporangium has oval capsule and multicellular stalk. The capsule wall consists of two distinct region; thick walled region known as annulus and thin walled region known as stomium. The capsule consists of 12-16 diploid spore mother cells.

Figure 2.5.3 Internal Structure of Sorus The spore mother cells undergo meiotic cell division to form 48-64 haploid spores. All the spores are of similar type hence, the plant is homosporous. 2. Sexual Reproduction: After maturation of spores, the capsule wall breaks at stomium and spores are dispersed. After falling on a suitable soil the spores germinate to gametophytic stage known as prothallus.

Figure 2.5.3 Structure of Prothallus The prothallus is haploid, dorsiventrally flattened, multicellular, green, heart shaped structure. It is monoecious i.e. male and female reproductive organs are present on same thallus. At the anterior portion it consists of apical notch. Ventral surface bear rhizoids which help in anchorage and absorption of water and nutrients from the soil. It is independent and the mode of nutrition is autotrophic. The female sex organs are developed near the apical notch while the male sex organs are developed at posterior rhizoidal region. An antheridium is a multicellular oval or rounded structure without stalk. It consists of androcytes which metamorphose into multiflagellate antherozoids or spermatozoids. The antheridial wall breaks when it absorbs water, then the antherozoids are liberated and are set free to swim in water. An archegonium is flask shaped; consist of large basal venter and narrow neck. The venter consists of large egg cell and venter canal cell. The neck consists of binucleate neck canal cell.

Figure 2.5.3 Structure of archegonium After maturation of archegonium, venter canal cell and neck canal cell disintegrate to form a passage. The passage is filled with mucilage and malic acid. The malic acid of archegonium attracts the swimming antherozoids liberated from antheridia. Some of them enter the passage of archegonium, but only one antherozoid fertilize with egg to form diploid zygote (Oospore). Although there are several archegonia in the prothallus only one is fertilized. The oospore is the beginning of sporophytic generation of fern plant. The zygote divides and redivides by mitotic cell division to form embryo, which later develops into sporophyte. Initially, the young sporophyte is fully dependent on prothallus. Once the roots are developed, the sporophyte becomes fully independent and then the prothallus disintegrates.
Figure 2.5.4 Life cycle of Dryopteris (fern) 2.6.4 ECONOMIC IMPORTANCE OF PTERIDOPHYTES Pteridophhtes are economically very important. Some are mentioned below:
1. Ornamental value: Many ferns are grown as ornamental plants in gardens for their large, showy and graceful foliage.

2. Food: Pteridophytes serve as a good source of animal food. The young leaf tips of ferns (like,Diplazium esculentum), the circinate ptyxis are used as vegetable. The rhizome of many ferns are rich in starch, is used as food.
3. Soil Binding: Pteridophytes prevent soil erosion by binding the soil even along hill slopes. Many pteridphytes species are used in soil conservation.
